book.title: The account in one page
book.text: Super73 is an e-bike brand that wants service to be what sets it apart. It pays about 18 outsourced agents to answer calls and emails through Zendesk. In Sep 2026 it signed a $6,000 a month order with Supernal for a voice agent that answers the phone, troubleshoots bikes and hands the rest to people. The agent is called Keith. Around him sit a knowledge layer and a Command Center where the client tests and later watches calls. The build is in week 8, testing with the client starts 17 Nov 2026 and launch is planned for late Jan 2027. Three people run it: Johnny on the relationship, Diana on strategy and product, Vitor on engineering.

book.title: Why they bought and how the deal is built
book.text: The introduction was personal: Drystone's CFO knew Super73's CFO. The case rested on several things at once. The outsourced team and two support tools cost about $46,600 a month. Calls peak beyond what 18 people can take. And the leadership wants a premium service experience. Taylor had 23 wishes but chose to test Supernal on one. The price is low for Supernal, a holdover from older pricing, on a six-month term that then runs monthly. The client owns the code. Minutes are included up to an allowance, then billed at cost. Every later lane needs its own order form, so this first build is the audition for a much larger account, put internally at $300,000 or more a year.
sources: Drive: 11 - Metrics master and cost model.md

book.title: The product and why it is built this way
book.text: The order form says “Tier 1 troubleshooting”. At Super73, Tier 1 means every first contact, whatever the topic. Diana and Vitor resolved this by making Keith the front door for all calls while resolving only troubleshooting, North America only. An audit of two months of tickets gave 15 paths Keith can finish, 10 he can part-finish and 3 that transfer at once for safety; the set later grew to 28. Because the client has detailed procedures, rules are coded per path and each step shows its source. A fast model with a retrieval tool was chosen because slower, smarter ones broke the conversation. The Command Center exists so the client can prove Keith before real callers meet him.
sources: Super73 <> Supernal, 29 Sep, 6 Oct and 3 Nov 2026

book.title: How delivery has gone and the people
book.text: Kickoff slipped a month from the planned date, and Supernal held the Nov target anyway. Discovery took four weeks and weekly milestones have mostly been met. MAC is the engine on the client side: he answers questionnaires, rules on conflicts in the knowledge base and reacts warmly to demos. Taylor signs and watches milestones. Bryson, the CFO, sits in. The strain is on Supernal's side. Vitor is split across two projects, a hosting incident cost time in Oct, and telephony has been the critical path since 20 Oct without a settled owner for the carrier account. MAC has warned Johnny that the COO and CFO expected more by now.

book.title: Where it stands and what is next
book.text: On 13 Nov 2026 the build is 56% against a 17 Nov date, with the fourth sub-milestone sign-off, the carrier account and the SMS registration all past due. Keith still reads mainly one SOP file and has not been tried at volume. The testing plan is agreed: core paths on the web, then by phone, then edge cases, with a first window for real calls around 18 Dec. Three things need a decision: who owns Twilio, how the minute allowance is read, and where the engine runs. If the first use case lands, order tracking is the obvious next path, and MAC is already talking about messaging and EU support.

answers.q: Is the 17 Nov build-complete date safe?
answers.a: Not clearly. On 13 Nov the build is 56% with SM4 sign-off, the carrier account and SMS registration past due. Telephony has been the critical path since 20 Oct without a settled owner for the Twilio account.

answers.q: Why is the price below Supernal’s minimum?
answers.a: The $6,000 a month was carried over from the old pricing model, below the $8,000 minimum. The first build is treated as an audition for a larger account, sized internally at $300,000 or more a year, with each later lane needing its own order form.

answers.q: What would the next expansion be?
answers.a: Order tracking, about 30% of calls, is the obvious next path once troubleshooting lands. MAC is already talking about messaging and EU support, and the order form names eight later lanes from warranty automation to NetSuite reporting.
